title: Evaluate‑and‑Repair for LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes: A Preregistered Generate–Verify–Repair Study with a Deterministic Net Verifier
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, within‑task paired experiment (N=300 canonical device change tasks: routing 150 / ACL 100 / BGP 50) that measured whether a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—an LLM proposer (gpt‑5‑mini) whose proposals are gated by a deterministic network verifier and, on rejection, given one automated repair iteration—reduces the acceptance of proposals that would create unsafe or policy‑violating sandbox states versus LLM‑only proposals. Design (frozen): paired binary outcome per task = would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied (verifier‑anchored); primary test = McNemar exact two‑sided; bootstrap 95% CI. Results: complete pairs = 300; baseline unsafe = 1/300 (0.3333%); guarded (GVR) unsafe = 0/300 (0.00%); paired absolute reduction = 0.003333 (0.3333 percentage points); McNemar p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The single baseline unsafe case (task‑000165) was repaired by the automated repair iteration; raw proposer outputs, verifier traces and repair call JSONs are archived (paths and hashes below). We preserve full execution provenance for deterministic replay and discuss verifier scope, practical implications, and limitations (single proposer model, canonical task bank, verifier coverage, and low baseline failure prevalence).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate operator intent into device configuration proposals, but stochastic generation risks producing changes that are syntactically plausible yet operationally unsafe (e.g., unintended reachability, weakened ACLs). Operational NetOps requires mechanistic patterns that convert probabilistic proposals into deterministic, auditable acceptance decisions. Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) architectures interpose deterministic verifiers as acceptance gates and feed structured counterexamples to the generator for repair. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001) to quantify whether a verifier gate plus one automated repair iteration reduces the rate of proposals that would cause unsafe sandbox states compared with LLM‑only proposals. Contributions: (1) a complete preregistered paired study with frozen decision rules and archived artifacts; (2) an implemented gated verifier + one‑iteration repair flow with an exemplar repaired episode archived; (3) an evidence bundle and discussion about operational implications and verifier limits.
sections.related_work: The study builds on generate–verify–repair concepts in LLM‑assisted code and compliance (e.g., Cadenas 2026 on GVR for deterministic correctness), RAG/verification surveys that show grounding reduces hallucinations (Gao et al., arXiv:2312.10997), and NetOps verification work that supplies deterministic checking primitives (Header‑space/SEFL/SymNet and static reachability tools). Recent agentic NetOps surveys emphasise assurance contracts, bounded tool scopes, and gated execution for safe autonomous action. Unlike prior descriptive surveys or single‑case engineering demonstrations, we preregistered a confirmatory, within‑task paired experiment with deterministic scoring and archived provenance to enable replayable audit.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration identifier is CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001 (SHA‑256: 156e87e6ce4a9a2348525fa8960f35fb4120031344cf4b4a38b247b10893181b). The preregistration froze task sampling, proposer model, verifier checks and thresholds, repair budget (≤1 automated repair invocation), estimands, analysis plan (McNemar exact two‑sided; 10k bootstrap for CI), missingness/exclusion rules, and stopping rules. Task bank and sampling. Deterministic stratified sampling (seed 2026‑08‑25) produced 300 canonical device tasks: routing (150), ACL (100), BGP (50). Proposer and orchestration. Proposer model: gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Model configuration and run harness are archived (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: a40e96e2..., execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256: 7df39740...). Verifier decision rules (frozen) and implementation are archived at execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: f3ac5460...). Outcome definition (frozen). Primary per‑task binary outcome = 'would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied' as determined by the deterministic verifier when the candidate change is hypothetically applied in the canonical sandbox. The verifier performs the following preregistered checks (enumerated and frozen prior to any model calls): 1) Reachability regression: header‑space style reachability comparison that flags newly reachable flows violating canonical reachability policy; 2) ACL/policy violation: an explicit policy rule transitions from DENY to ALLOW for traffic classified as protected by canonical policy; 3) Parse/semantic invalidity: generated patch unparseable or semantically invalid in the canonical device model; 4) Deterministic safety predicates: mandated connectivity removals or non‑reversible control‑plane changes are flagged unsafe. These checks and thresholds were fixed and archived before execution. Guarded flow and repair loop. Guarded (GVR) flow: proposer→verifier; on rejection, verifier returns a structured counterexample; proposer is re‑invoked once with the counterexample appended as repair context (repair budget = 1). All raw proposer outputs, parsed canonical patches, verifier traces, and repair provider calls were logged and archived. Statistical analysis (frozen). Primary test: McNemar exact two‑sided on paired binary outcomes (discordant b=n_10, c=n_01); report absolute/relative reduction and exact p. Bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) for 95% percentile CI on paired absolute difference. All artifacts and scripts preserved for deterministic replay.

sections.discussion: Interpretation. The gated GVR flow corrected the single verifier‑detectable unsafe baseline proposal (task‑000165), showing that verifier gates plus short repair loops can eliminate verifier‑visible hazards in our canonical sandbox. The observed baseline failure prevalence was very low (1/300), so statistical sensitivity to modest absolute reductions is limited; the McNemar p=1.00 and the bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01] reflect that rarity. Operational implications. Where verifier‑visible failure classes dominate (reachability regressions, ACL policy flips, parse errors), gating proposals with a deterministic verifier and applying automated repairs can reduce verifier‑detectable hazards and provide auditable acceptance traces. Production adoption requires (i) expanding verifier semantics to vendor‑specific behaviors and multi‑change interactions, (ii) defining escalation and rollback policies for verifier‑out‑of‑scope cases, and (iii) larger experiments on higher‑risk change distributions. Threats to validity and limitations. Internal validity: single proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini) and single verifier implementation; prompt sensitivity and model nondeterminism are logged (provider call archives). Construct validity: the primary outcome depends on verifier capability and coverage (verifier rules archived at execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: f3ac5460...). External validity: canonical tasks differ from heterogeneous production change streams. Conclusion validity: rare baseline failures yield wide uncertainty; results are a reproducible mechanistic proof‑of‑concept rather than production readiness proof. Future work: multi‑model experiments, expanded verifier coverage (vendor semantics, multi‑change safety properties), and canary trials with human‑in‑loop escalation.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered paired experiment (N=300) demonstrates that a deterministic verifier gate plus a single automated repair iteration can correct a verifier‑detectable unsafe LLM proposal in a canonical NetOps sandbox (observed baseline 1/300 → guarded 0/300). Observed paired absolute reduction = 0.003333 (0.3333 percentage points); McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The run validates reproducible GVR mechanics and provides a complete archived artifact corpus for deterministic replay and audit. Broader operational claims require follow‑on studies with higher baseline hazard rates, multiple proposer models, and extended verifier semantics. All artifacts, logs, verifier rules and analysis scripts required to reproduce the confirmatory table and statistics are archived and hashed (see Disclosure).

limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used a single proposer (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Canonical task bank: tasks were deterministic canonical templates (routing, ACL, BGP); production change distributions may differ materially and have higher baseline failure rates.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier models a canonical subset (reachability regressions, ACL/policy flips, parse/semantic invalidity, mandated‑connectivity removals) but omits some vendor‑specific coupled behaviors and multi‑change interactions (verifier implementation and decision rules archived: execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: f3ac5460...).
Low baseline failure prevalence: only 1/300 baseline unsafe proposals were observed, limiting statistical power and widening uncertainty for modest absolute reductions.

Sandbox abstraction: the canonical sandbox is a model of device semantics for deterministic checking and is not a substitute for vendor device execution; production deployment requires extended validation on vendor devices and in live canary trials.
